teaser: He turns his head away from you and stares you down at the same time.
review_notes:
Medium: oil and opaque color on wood, about 32 x 40 cm.
Pendant to Portrait of Wally Neuzil (1912), also Leopold Museum.
Neulengbach arrest in April 1912, 24 days in custody, a drawing burned by the judge in court: standard account.
Portrait of Wally seized in New York in 1998 after a MoMA loan; settled in 2010 for 19 million dollars: verify figure.
Schiele left the Vienna Academy in 1909.

lesson.text: The head turns away, toward the right edge. The eyes do the opposite and swing back to pin you. The chin is lifted like a man who feels superior, yet the skin is bruised with blue, red and green as if he had been hit. Egon Schiele is 22 here, and he paints himself as proud and wounded in the same face.

The contradiction continues in the format. A portrait is usually upright, like a standing person. Schiele turns the panel on its side, like a landscape, and then pushes himself off center. One shoulder rises high, the other drops out of sight. The top of his hair is sliced away by the frame.
That imbalance is deliberate. Schiele planned it as carefully as another painter would plan symmetry, and it can be traced in a few strokes.
Three lines show how unstable Schiele makes his own portrait.

lines.label: A slipping shoulder line
lines.text: His left shoulder sits high and square on the right. The other side slides down to the bottom corner. The black torso tilts like a boat taking on water.

lines.label: The twisted neck
lines.text: Head and neck lean one way while the body leans the other. It is a pose you could not hold for long, and you feel the strain.

lines.label: The stem
lines.text: On the empty side, a thin stalk curves like a question mark. It is as fragile as the black shape is heavy, and it balances the picture.

lesson.text: So a dry twig weighs as much as a man. Schiele learned this from his mentor, Gustav Klimt, and from Japanese prints, which both loved empty space and off-center subjects. But Klimt filled his backgrounds with gold. Schiele leaves his bare: thick whitish paint, brushed in all directions, like a wall he is pressed against.

The panel is tiny: about 32 by 40 centimeters, close to a sheet of office paper laid sideways. And it is wood, not canvas. Schiele painted on it with oil and with opaque, chalky color, which lets the brush marks stay dry and scratchy.
On such a small surface, every mark counts. The jacket is a flat dark mass and the wall a pale blur. Move in on the face, where he spends the most paint and the most colors.

lesson.title: A face under pressure
lesson.text: The skin is where Schiele breaks hardest with tradition.

spots.title: Two unequal eyes
spots.text: One eye is wide and dark, fixed on you. The other is narrower, half in shadow near the edge of the face. The heavy brows are arched, almost mocking.

spots.title: Skin like a map
spots.text: Strokes of blue, green, violet and rust run across cheek and jaw. Schiele is not coloring a face. He is exposing nerves, veins and bone under it.

spots.title: The ear
spots.text: A big ear, red at the rim, sticks out against the pale ground. Its outline is drawn in a thin dark line, as sharp as in his drawings.

lesson.text: Schiele was first of all a draftsman, someone who thinks in line. He had walked out of the Vienna Academy in 1909, tired of copying plaster casts. Even in paint, he draws: the edge of the jaw, the collar, the ear are contours filled in afterward. The color is added like a fever on top of the drawing.
Against all this gray, black and bruised flesh, a single pure color is used twice. Once for the plant, where you cannot miss it. And once somewhere else, in a much smaller dose.
The lanterns of the plant are bright red-orange. Where on Schiele himself does that same red return?

spots.title: The lips
spots.text: His mouth is painted in the red of the lanterns, slightly parted. Plant and man are tied by one color: both are alive, and both are already drying out.

lesson.text: The plant is a physalis, called Chinese lantern for the papery orange husks that wrap its fruit. It turns red in the fall, as the leaves wither. Here some lanterns glow while the leaves beside them have gone brown and curled. Schiele, obsessed with decay even at 22, found in it a portrait of himself.

The year 1912 was brutal for him. In April he was arrested in the small town of Neulengbach and held for 24 days. The most serious charges were dropped, but he was convicted of displaying erotic drawings where children could see them, and the judge burned one of his drawings in the courtroom.

This picture has a twin. In the same year, on a panel of the same size, Schiele painted his companion and model Wally Neuzil, her head tilted the opposite way, a spray of leaves behind her. Hung side by side, the two lean toward each other. Both now belong to the Leopold Museum in Vienna.

Wally's portrait took a long detour. Lent to New York in 1997, it was seized by American authorities as art looted by a Nazi from its Jewish owner, the dealer Lea Bondi Jaray. After twelve years of legal battle, the museum paid her heirs 19 million dollars in 2010 to bring it home.
Schiele makes imbalance the subject: a tilted body, an empty half, mismatched eyes. The portrait shows no settled character, only a young man holding a pose he can barely keep.

quiz.question: What is unusual about the format of this portrait?
options: It is wider than tall, like a landscape
quiz.explanation: Schiele turns the panel sideways and places himself off center.

quiz.question: What balances the heavy black torso?
options: A thin plant stem on the empty side
quiz.explanation: The fragile curved stalk on the left answers the dark mass on the right.

quiz.question: Where does the red of the lanterns reappear?
quiz.explanation: His mouth is painted in the same red-orange as the plant.

quiz.question: What happened to Schiele in April 1912?
options: He won a prize from the Academy
He was arrested and held for 24 days
quiz.explanation: He was jailed in Neulengbach, and a judge burned one of his drawings.

quiz.question: Which painting is the twin of this self-portrait?
quiz.explanation: He painted Wally the same year on a panel of the same size.

facts.text: The painting is about as large as a door.
facts.explanation: It is tiny, about 32 by 40 centimeters.

facts.text: Schiele's head and eyes point in different directions.
facts.explanation: The head turns away while the eyes swing back to the viewer.

facts.text: The background is covered in gold leaf, as in Klimt's portraits.
facts.explanation: Schiele leaves it bare, in thick whitish paint.
